newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal sees revenue hike in 97 budget plan.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal sees revenue hike in 97 budget plan.

text.p: The Portuguese government's draft 1997 budget presented to opposition parties on Friday forecasts a strong boost to revenues and a tight lid on spending to meet tough entry conditions for joining a single European currency.
The draft, which implies a "strong limitation" of public spending, saw spending rising 4.5 percent year-on-year, the Finance Ministry said. Receipts would rise nine percent.

The budget proposals outlined savings of 200 billion escudos ($1.3 billion) compared with 1996, with the deficit narrowing to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from an expected 4.3 percent this year, the Finance Ministry said.
Portugal is trying to meet the European Union's requirement for it to cut its budget deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997 in order to qualify to join the single currency in 1999.
"Even if Portugal does not cut its budget deficit to 2.9 percent next year, it should be close," said Keith Edmonds, economist with IBJ International in London.

State spending on goods and services would fall due to the tight controls being applied to the ministries, the Finance Ministry said. The Education Ministry would be one of the few ministries to see a rise in spending.
The budget proposals were based on expectations of increased tax collection efficiency, departmental spending cuts, higher economic growth and lower debt servicing costs, economists said.

Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco has promised no tax increases for a second straight year in 1997 and said on Friday the budget proposals included a reduction in corporate tax of up to two percentage points to 34 percent.
He said the government expected to earn 450 billion escudos from privatisations in 1997, around the same level as expected this year.
Sally Wilkinson, economist with UBS in London, said: "The budget is a little optimistic in terms of growth and revenue assumptions, and presents no major new structural measures."
IBJ's Edmonds said : "The government has had success in improving tax collection efficiency, and this should continue."
The government has said it would crack down on widespread tax evasion in order to boost revenues.
Companies are under strong pressure from the government to meet their tax arrears, economists said.

"It would have been counter-productive to have had an aggressive cost-cutting budget. If the government started slashing public sector employment, it would end up with weaker growth and lower tax receipts," Wilkinson said.
The draft budget will be formally approved by the cabinet on Monday and sent to parliament the following day. Analysts expect the budget to be passed in a vote in November.
The budget proposal forecasts that the weight of state spending as a percentage of GDP will fall to 28.7 percent from 29 percent this year.

The government had already announced the macro-economic forecasts on which its budget was being based. These include economic growth next year of 2.75-3.25 percent, slightly higher than in 1996, and inflation of 2.0-2.25 percent, down from a forecast 3.0-3.5 percent in 1996.
Debt interest payments would fall to 14.5 percent of GDP from 15.7 percent this year.

State investment would rise 10 percent in nominal terms to 441.3 billion escudos. Public consumption is seen rising more slowly than in 1996 at 0.75-1.25 percent while private consumption should rise 2.0-2.5 percent.
